verses.text: King Ben Hadad of Syria gathered his whole army, along with thirty-two allied kings and their horses and chariots. He laid siege to Samaria and attacked it.
He sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel. They told him, “This is what Ben Hadad says:
‘Your silver and gold are mine, and so are the best of your wives and children.’”
The king of Israel answered, “As you say, my lord the king. I belong to you, and so does everything I have.”
The messengers came back and said, “Ben Hadad says, ‘I already demanded that you hand over your silver and gold, your wives, and your children.
Around this time tomorrow I'll send my servants to search your palace and your officials' houses. They'll take away everything you value.’”
Then the king of Israel called all the elders of the land. “See how this man is looking for trouble,” he said. “He demanded my wives, my children, my silver, and my gold, and I didn't turn him down.”
All the elders and the people told him, “Don't listen to him. Don't agree to this.”
So Ahab told Ben Hadad's messengers, “Tell my lord the king, ‘I'll do everything you first asked of your servant, but I can't do this.’” The messengers took the answer back to Ben Hadad.
Ben Hadad sent back this reply: “May the gods punish me severely if there's enough dust left in Samaria for each man following me to take a handful.”
The king of Israel answered, “Tell him, ‘A man putting on his armor shouldn't boast like a man taking it off.’”
When Ben Hadad heard the message, he and the other kings were drinking in their shelters. He told his men, “Get ready to attack!” So they took their positions against the city.
A prophet came to Ahab king of Israel and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘See this huge army? I'm handing it over to you today. Then you'll know that I am the LORD.’”
“Through whom?” Ahab asked. The prophet replied, “The LORD says, ‘Through the young men serving the provincial officials.’” Ahab asked, “Who should start the battle?” The prophet answered, “You.”
Ahab called up the young men who served the provincial officials. There were two hundred and thirty-two of them. Then he called up the rest of the Israelite troops, seven thousand in all.
They marched out at noon. By then Ben Hadad and the thirty-two kings helping him were getting drunk in their shelters.
The young men serving the provincial officials went out first. Ben Hadad sent scouts out, and they reported, “Men are coming out of Samaria.”
He said, “Whether they've come out for peace or for battle, take them alive.”
The young men serving the provincial officials came out of the city with the army behind them.
Each struck down the man he faced. The Syrians ran, and Israel chased them. King Ben Hadad of Syria escaped on horseback with some horsemen.
The king of Israel went out, struck the horses and chariots, and inflicted heavy losses on the Syrians.
Then the prophet came to the king of Israel and told him, “Go strengthen your forces and decide what you need to do. When the year comes around again, the king of Syria will attack you.”
The king of Syria's officials told him, “Their god is a god of the hills. That's why they were stronger than us. If we fight them on the plain, we'll surely be stronger than they are.
Here's what to do. Remove the kings from their commands and put officers in their places.
Raise an army like the one you lost, horse for horse and chariot for chariot. We'll fight them on the plain and surely overpower them.” The king listened and did what they said.
When the year came around again, Ben Hadad gathered the Syrian army and went up to Aphek to fight Israel.
The Israelites were called up, given supplies, and sent out to meet them. Israel camped opposite them like two little flocks of young goats, while the Syrians filled the land.

A man of God came to the king of Israel and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Because the Syrians say the LORD is a god of the hills and has no power in the valleys, I'll hand this entire army over to you. Then you'll know that I am the LORD.’”
The two armies camped opposite each other for seven days. On the seventh day the battle began, and the Israelites struck down a hundred thousand Syrian foot soldiers in a single day.
The survivors ran into the city of Aphek, and its wall collapsed on twenty-seven thousand of them. Ben Hadad escaped into the city and hid in an inner room.
His officials told him, “We've heard that Israel's kings are merciful. Let us put sackcloth around our bodies and ropes on our heads and go out to the king of Israel. Maybe he'll let you live.”
They put on sackcloth and ropes and went to the king of Israel. “Your servant Ben Hadad says, ‘Please let me live,’” they said. Ahab replied, “Is he still alive? He's my brother.”

The men were watching for any sign of mercy and latched onto his words. “Your brother Ben Hadad,” they said. “Go bring him,” Ahab replied. When Ben Hadad came out to him, Ahab invited him up into his chariot.

Ben Hadad told him, “I'll give back the towns my father took from yours. You can set up trading streets in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria.” Ahab said, “I'll release you under that agreement.” So he made a treaty with him and let him go.
One of the members of the prophets' company told another at the LORD's command, “Please strike me.” The man refused.
The prophet told him, “Because you didn't obey the LORD's voice, a lion will kill you as soon as you leave me.” As soon as the man left, a lion found him and killed him.
The prophet found another man and said, “Please strike me.” The man struck him and wounded him.
The prophet then stood beside the road to wait for the king. He disguised himself by pulling his headband down over his eyes.

As the king passed by, the prophet called out to him: “I went into the middle of the battle, and someone brought me a prisoner. He told me, ‘Guard this man. If he gets away, you'll pay with your life or a talent of silver.’
While I was busy here and there, the prisoner slipped away.” The king of Israel answered, “That's your sentence, then. You've pronounced it yourself.”
The man quickly pulled the headband off his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets.

He told the king, “This is what the LORD says: ‘You let the man I had set apart for destruction slip out of your hands. Your life will take the place of his life, and your people will take the place of his people.’”
The king of Israel went home to Samaria sullen and angry.
